name: OneNote
tagline: Microsoft's freeform notebook app: notebooks, sections and pages you can type, ink or paste anything into.

pricing.plan: Free, with fuller features via Microsoft 365
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. OneNote itself is free to use and the paid angle is the Microsoft 365 bundle, so a standalone monthly figure is not meaningful.

verdictSummary: The data model here is not exotic: notebooks contain sections, sections contain pages, pages contain rich text and images. An agent can hand you a local notes app with that hierarchy, full text search and a real editor in one sitting, and for a lot of people that covers 90 percent of actual OneNote use. What it will not hand you is the part Microsoft actually spent twenty years on: silent sync across five devices, pen and palm rejection on a tablet, handwriting search, OCR inside pasted screenshots, and the Outlook and Teams plumbing. Also worth saying out loud: OneNote is free, so the DIY case is about owning your files rather than saving money. Build it if you want plain data on your own disk, not because the bill hurts.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app with a notebook/section/page tree, a rich text editor that accepts pasted images, and instant full text search over everything, all stored in a SQLite file you own.
requirements: Local disk for the SQLite file and image attachments
Optional: a synced folder or private git repo if you want the database on more than one machine
whatYouLose: Real cross-device sync with conflict handling, including the phone and tablet apps
Pen input that behaves: ink layers, palm rejection, lasso select, handwriting search
OCR on pasted screenshots and PDFs, so your image text stops being searchable
Outlook, Teams and Office integrations, meeting notes capture, Web Clipper
Shared notebooks with live multi-user editing and permissions
moatNotes: Years of accumulated notebooks in a proprietary-ish format is its own gravity well, and the pen experience is closer to hardware work than app work.
whyPeopleStillPay: Almost nobody pays for OneNote directly; they pay for Microsoft 365 and OneNote comes along, which is exactly why it survives. It is already installed, already signed in, already syncing, and it is the only note app that treats a stylus as a first class citizen rather than a gimmick. People also stay because the notebooks are enormous and old, and migrating a decade of clipped pages and inked meeting notes into anything else is a project nobody schedules.
notes: Rare case where the DIY pitch is data ownership, not price. If you use a pen, stop reading and stay put.
prompt:
Build a local-first freeform notes app called "Notebook" that replaces basic OneNote use for one person.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 (App Router) with TypeScript, run locally with `npm run dev`.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, single file at ./data/notebook.db.
- TipTap for the editor.
- Tailwind for styling. No component library.
- No auth, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics. Single user on localhost.

Data model:
- notebooks (id, name, order)
- sections (id, notebook_id, name, order)
- pages (id, section_id, title, content_json, content_text, created_at, updated_at)
- attachments (id, page_id, filename, mime) with bytes written to ./data/attachments/
- Use an FTS5 virtual table over pages.title and pages.content_text.

UI:
- Three panes: notebook/section tree on the left, page list in the middle, editor on the right. Resizable is nice, not required.
- Editor supports headings, bold/italic/code, bullet and numbered lists, checkboxes, tables, code blocks, and inline images.
- Paste an image from the clipboard: save the bytes to ./data/attachments/, insert it inline. This must work, it is the main reason people use OneNote.
- Autosave on a 500ms debounce. Never show a save button.
- Cmd/Ctrl+K opens a search palette that queries FTS5 and jumps to the matching page with the term highlighted.
- Rename, reorder and delete for notebooks, sections and pages. Deletes go to a trash section, not oblivion.

Also build:
- `npm run export`: dumps every page as Markdown into ./export/notebook/section/page.md with attachments copied alongside. This is the escape hatch, treat it as a feature.
- A README with setup, where the data lives, and how to back it up.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: stylus/ink capture, OCR, multi-device sync, sharing, mobile apps, Outlook or Office integration.

No secrets are needed. If you add any config, put it in .env.local and commit .env.example only.
When done, seed one notebook with two sections and three sample pages so the app is not empty on first run.
